newsitem.title: UK: BA invites cabin crew talks with arbitrator.
newsitem.headline: BA invites cabin crew talks with arbitrator.

text.p: British Airways Plc said its chief executive Bob Ayling has written to the Transport and General Workers Union (T&G) general secretary Bill Morris to suggest opening talks on the cabin crew dispute with the assistance of an independent arbitrator.

Michael Blunt, BA's head of corporate communications, told Reuters the suggestion was made in a letter which was sent to Morris just before the T&G gave the go-ahead to a cabin crew strike next week. Blunt also said BA was still confident that talks with ground staff over another dispute could be resolved within 48 hours.
Blunt said the use of an independent arbitrator had helped resolve last year's pilots strike threat and proved to be a good idea. "We said why don't we adopt the same approach again."
The T&G gave its backing to BA cabin crew strike action earlier on Tuesday, after those balloted had voted overwhelmingly in favour of action last week.

The cabin crew row centres on a five-month-long pay dispute. BA also faces a separate row with ground staff, who voted in favour of striking on Monday and are still deciding whether to push ahead with industrial action.
The ground staff dispute is based on BA's decision to sell its catering business, which employs around 1,200 staff.
Both issues stem from BA's efforts to cut costs in a restructuring effort to axe one billion pounds ($1.7 billion) by the year 2000.
BA said whatever the outcome of the talks and threats, it had already put into place contingency plans to keep services flying out of Heathrow and Gatwick airport if it was hit by disruption.
Blunt refused to comment on how much these plans were costing the group. But analysts said last year's threat of a pilot strike cost BA upwards of 10 million pounds. ($ = 0.600 British Pounds)
